this film did not work for me. the social commentary only really works, i think, if you bought into it ahead of time and are actively looking for it in the text. the (uncharismatic, irritating) hypnotist's victims aren't sufficiently fleshed out to support the idea that through subtle manipulation he's dredging up murderous misanthropic desires simmering beneath the surface of our alienated modern culture. it just looks like magic brainwashing. there's the implied horror, i suppose, of the fundamental unknowability of other people and even your own self, of what you are capable of thinking and doing under the right circumstances, but i just don't think the film actually conveys that in a compelling way. the first half drags. it's repetitive and kinda boring, showing the hypnotist's "method" over and over in a way that doesn't really build up to much. the second half is more entertaining to watch, but it's both too concrete to leave much up to interpretation and too abstract to set up and resolve the mystery, such as it was, in a satisfying way. the depiction of hypnosis stretched my suspension of disbelief thin, all in service of something that wasn't terrifying enough to instinctually scare or relatable enough to evoke a more conscious, intellectual dread. the film does some interesting stuff from a technical perspective, but that wasn't enough to hook me. tbh reading through the reviews i got the impression that either i watched a different film to everyone else, or the audience is 95% film students

The influences that contributed to this and also what came from it are very apparent, but unfortunately, this just did not work for me. I found it to be unbearably slow and uninteresting, and that’s coming from someone who often times appreciates a slower pace in film. What lost me on this was mainly the story; it was confusing and subtle in a way that the vagueness just made me continuously stay more and more unengaged as it went on. I found the character of Mamiya to be very frustrating and the long, drawn out scenes of his repetitiveness over and over again I really just disliked. I don’t know, I know a lot of people praise highly of this film and while I went in truly wanting to love it, I just never had that moment of connection. Kurosawa’s 2024 film “Chime” (which I was told was a spiritual successor this film) I think worked a lot better with its condensed runtime and modern filmmaking techniques. Although from a technical perspective, I found the production quality to be high and I also enjoyed the performances from the cast. This isn’t going to be something I revisit because I don’t see myself having a better experience but I’m glad those that get it, get it.

Every conversation with the villain was the same conversation over and over again, and while it worked really well the first time, it got really repetitive and uninteresting after the 8th time. And by the time you get to the final act, the story really has nowhere to go except for where you expect it to. I love the bursts of violence, I love the cold drone that simmers on the soundtrack, and I think it’s occasionally pretty effective. But it’s more of a repetitive slog than anything else. They don’t make sweaters like they used to. The primal urge to kill; just a flicker away. The terror of losing control and hurting the ones you love. The psychological as inseparable from the supernatural. Hypnotic, haunting, deeply unsettling. One of those movies that feels cursed to watch. Unfolds slowly, with a cold sense of inevitability. The assurance that you will snap someday; not a matter of ‘if’ but ‘when.’ The fire awakens something within you, an urge that has existed since the dawn of mankind. Maybe its influence is demonic in nature, maybe it’s baked into our DNA. A film too blackly intelligent to offer any easy answers or explanations; and besides, you know the truth anyway, don’t you? You’re just terrified to admit it to yourself. Kiyoshi Kurosawa is surely one of the best living writer-directors, a fact I am certain of even with this being my first film from him. A master of tone, pacing, storytelling; complete confidence in shot length, thematic subtlety, and a respect for the viewer to piece together information on their own. Beautiful, uneasy cinematography. Uses angles, windows, doorways, and distance to keep the viewer from the characters. You feel the urge to lean in, as if you’re an eavesdropper who just caught a glimpse of a strange conversation from across the beach. Long shots to prolong tension and deny release; to invite speculation, to sit with characters in moments of illogic and bewilderment. Koji Yakusho is one of the best living actors, full stop. He knows how to internalize his character’s emotions, convey changes in subtle ways, and go “big” and fully external when the story calls for it. Seeing him in a leading role is almost a seal of quality that the movie is going to be superb. This is not to discredit the work of his costars, whose work is on equal footing with his own, especially Masato Hagiwara, who gives one of the most skin-crawling performances I’ve ever seen in horror. As I was watching this, I didn’t want it to end. I know for a fact I’m going to rewatch this movie many times again, and I bet that I’ll get more out of it with each successive viewing. Its terrifying questions and insights into human psychology will stay with you long after the credits roll. This is unquestionably one of the greatest masterpieces in horror film history. Essential viewing. Mesmerizing.

Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Cure (1997) stands out for its extraordinary visual language, particularly in its use of light and shadow. The way a single drop of water falls onto a lighter is quite literally "mesmerizing". I didn't know about the German physician and philosopher Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), who believed in an invisible "magnetic fluid" whose blockage caused illness, making him one of the intellectual precursors of modern hypnosis. In fact, the English verb to mesmerize is an eponym derived directly from his name. The story follows detective Kenichi Takabe and the psychiatrist Sakuma as they investigate a series of gruesome murders in which each victim has an "X" carved into the neck. The perpetrators all seem bizarrely detached from their actions, unable to explain why they killed. Takabe eventually suspects the mysterious drifter Mamiya, a former psychology student who had researched Mesmer before apparently losing his memory. A psychological cat-and-mouse game unfolds, although Mamiya is unable to fully hypnotize Takabe in the same way he manipulates everyone else. Instead, he gradually implants doubt, fragmented memories, and partial illusions into his mind. The film's fascination with identity, memory, and suggestion inevitably recalls Christopher Nolan's Memento and Inception, for which Cure may well have served as an important inspiration. Meanwhile, Sakuma articulates a classic axiom of hypnosis: that people only perform actions under hypnosis that they secretly wanted to do anyway. In psychoanalytic terms, one could argue that hypnosis merely releases the repressed drives of the Id rather than inventing a new personality. However, this creates a dilemma. The killers are all remarkably ordinary people: a husband who seemingly loved his wife, a doctor, a police officer annoyed by his colleague. None of them appear liberated after the murders; instead, they seem confused, detached, horrified by what they have done. This forces us to question whether Sakuma is wrong, or whether the film is testing the disturbing hypothesis that the average modern subject is inherently psychopathic, or at least that beneath ordinary social identities lies an unexpected capacity for violence. The title Cure thus becomes a dark irony. Mamiya mayben sees himself as a healer, someone who "cures" people of their socially constructed selves through hypnosis and violence. Rather than revealing authentic freedom, however, he dissolves identity itself, leaving only alienation and murder behind. In the end, much like in Se7en, which Kurosawa himself has cited as an inspiration, Mamiya practically orchestrates his own death. By pulling the trigger, Takabe seemingly falls into Mamiya's trap. He succumbs to the very violence he has spent the entire film investigating. He shoots Mamiya three times, briefly speaks as if he has won, and then calmly fires five more bullets into his body. As the chilling final scene in the restaurant suggests, the "cure" was never about Mamiya himself. It has simply found a new host.

"All the things that used to be inside of me… now they are all outside." Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Cure is one of the most quietly disturbing films ever made... an absolute masterpiece of psychological horror, existential dread, and suffocating restraint. On the surface it’s a serial‑killer procedural, even sharing DNA with Fincher’s brilliant Se7en, but Kurosawa uses the genre only as a skeleton. What he builds on top of it is a bleak, nihilistic examination of human vulnerability, the erosion of identity, and the terrifying idea that violence isn’t imposed from outside circumstance, but awakened from within. The story follows Detective Takabe (Kōji Yakusho), a man already stretched thin by his wife’s worsening mental illness and the emotional exhaustion of his job. His life is a fragile balancing act, and Kurosawa uses that instability as the perfect entry point for the film’s central horror: a series of murders committed by everyday ordinary people who have no motive, no memory, and no explanation. Their only connection is a wandering drifter named Mamiya (Masato Hagiwara), whose vacant stare and fragmented speech seem to hollow out the minds of everyone he encounters. Mamiya doesn’t kill... he just removes the part of people that resists killing. Kurosawa’s direction is astonishingly controlled. The pacing is glacial, the dialogue sparse, the atmosphere suffocating. Every scene feels slightly askew, as if reality itself is losing structural integrity. The cinematography is incredible: long static shots, oppressive negative space, and a washed‑out palette that makes Tokyo look like a decaying Silent Hill‑esque purgatory. Kurosawa weaponizes emptiness... rooms feel too large, hallways too long, silence too loud. The sound design is equally unnerving, filled with distant hums, mechanical drones, and the constant threat of nothing happening at all. It’s a film where the absence of action becomes the source of tension and dread. Yakusho’s performance is extraordinary. He plays Takabe with a brittle mix of intensity and (seeming) restraint... a man whose sense of self is eroding under the weight of responsibility and despair. His exhaustion becomes the emotional anchor of the film, making his slow descent into obsession and madness terrifying. Hagiwara’s Mamiya is the perfect counterpoint: airy, spacey, disturbingly serene. He’s not a villain in any traditional sense: he’s a void, a philosophical black hole that strips people down to their most primitive impulses. His presence evokes the same chilling inevitability as Anton Chigurh in No Country for Old Men, but filtered through a soft, almost childlike haze. The horror Kurosawa taps into feels even more potent today, where cycles of copycat violence (especially in the wake of high‑profile school shootings) show how fragile the boundary is between suggestion and action. Mamiya’s vacant presence unlocking buried impulses mirrors how real‑world perpetrators often inspire others not through ideology, but through a kind of psychological permission structure: the realization that someone else has crossed the line makes the line feel permeable. It’s deeply disturbing to recognize how prevalent violent urges are in humanity, how easily they can be awakened, and how quickly they spread when people see their own private darkness reflected in someone else’s public act. Cure forces us to confront the terrifying possibility that the capacity for violence is a dormant part of the human condition waiting for the right fracture. What makes Cure so remarkable is its refusal to offer answers. Kurosawa isn’t interested in explaining Mamiya’s methods or providing a neat psychological theory. Instead, he suggests something far more unsettling: that identity is fragile, morality is performative, and the boundary between self and suggestion is terrifyingly thin. The film becomes a meditation on how ordinary people justify extraordinary horrors, how violence blooms in the cracks of everyday life, and how the desire for meaning can lead to annihilation of self and others. It’s a worldview so depressingly bleak... and its quiet repression fits the late‑90s Japanese cultural landscape far more poignantly than the loud, chaotic spectacle of the modern American out-in-the-open bumfight/rainbet/pump.fun/Kalshi slop-filled attention economy. Cure works because it fuses philosophical horror, exquisite procedural mystery, and methodical atmospheric filmmaking into a hypnotic descent into existential terror. It’s deeply unsettling, thought‑provoking, and instantly one of the best films I’ve ever seen. Kurosawa understands that the violence lurking inside all of us (whether it ever emerges or not) is far scarier than any sort of monster or demon.
